topics.name: Huygens' Principle: Wavefronts, and Reflection and Refraction Using Wavefronts
topics.summary: A wavefront is a surface on which every point oscillates in the same phase, and a ray is always perpendicular to it. A point source gives spherical wavefronts, a line source gives cylindrical ones, and a very distant source gives plane wavefronts. Huygens' principle says every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread with the wave speed; the new wavefront a short time later is the common tangent (forward envelope) to all these wavelets. Applied at a boundary, the construction gives the law of reflection (equal speeds on both sides of the construction) and Snell's law of refraction, \( \sin i/\sin r=v_1/v_2 \). Light entering a denser medium slows down, \( v=c/\mu \), so the wavelets inside cover less distance and the ray bends toward the normal. This is the opposite of the old corpuscular theory, which needed light to speed up in a denser medium. Frequency never changes on refraction; speed and wavelength both fall by the factor \( \mu \).
topics.worked_example: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass with \( \mu=1.5 \). Speed in glass: \( v=\dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{1.5}=2\times10^{8} \) m/s. Wavelength in glass: \( \dfrac{600}{1.5}=400 \) nm. The frequency is unchanged, and because the wave slows down, the ray bends toward the normal.
common_mistakes: Saying light speeds up in a denser medium (the corpuscular-theory error)
Taking the new wavefront as the sum or average of the wavelets instead of their common tangent envelope
Thinking wavelength stays constant on refraction; it is frequency that stays constant
Inverting the speed ratio in Snell's law

topics.name: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
topics.summary: Interference is the superposition of light from two coherent sources, which have the same frequency and a constant phase difference. Independent lamps are incoherent because their phase difference changes randomly, so their fringes are never seen. In Young's double slit experiment, two slits lit by the same wavefront act as coherent sources. A bright fringe forms where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, \( \Delta=n\lambda \), and a dark fringe forms where \( \Delta=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda \). The centre, with zero path difference, is always bright. Fringe width \( \beta=\lambda D/d \) increases with wavelength and screen distance and decreases as the slit separation increases, so red light gives wider fringes than blue. With two equal sources of intensity \( I_0 \), the bright fringes reach \( 4I_0 \) and the dark ones reach zero. In a medium, \( \beta \) shrinks by the factor \( \mu \). A thin sheet over one slit shifts the whole pattern toward that slit by \( (\mu-1)tD/d \).
topics.worked_example: With \( \lambda=600 \) nm, \( d=0.5 \) mm and \( D=1 \) m: \( \beta=\dfrac{600\times10^{-9}\times1}{0.5\times10^{-3}}=1.2 \) mm. The third bright fringe is at \( 3\beta=3.6 \) mm from the centre, and the third dark fringe is at \( 2.5\beta=3 \) mm.
common_mistakes: Swapping the bright and dark conditions
Thinking a larger \( d \) gives wider fringes
Thinking red light gives narrower fringes than blue
Adding intensities (\( 2I_0 \)) instead of amplitudes (\( 4I_0 \)) at a bright fringe

topics.name: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
topics.summary: Diffraction is the bending of light into the geometrical shadow when it passes an edge or a narrow opening; it is noticeable when the opening is comparable to the wavelength. For a single slit of width \( a \), every point across the slit sends out secondary wavelets. Straight ahead they all arrive in phase, giving a bright central maximum. The condition \( a\sin\theta=n\lambda \) with \( n=\pm1,\pm2,\ldots \) gives the MINIMA, because the slit can then be split into parts whose wavelets cancel in pairs. This looks like Young's bright-fringe condition, but for a single slit it marks dark fringes. Secondary maxima lie roughly midway, at \( a\sin\theta=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda \), and are much dimmer. The central maximum spans from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other, so its angular width is \( 2\lambda/a \), twice the width \( \lambda/a \) of each secondary maximum. A narrower slit or longer wavelength spreads the pattern out. Ray optics holds only well within the Fresnel distance \( a^2/\lambda \).
topics.worked_example: For \( \lambda=500 \) nm, \( a=0.5 \) mm and a screen 1 m away, the first minimum is at \( \dfrac{\lambda D}{a}=1 \) mm from the centre, so the central maximum is \( 2 \) mm wide, while each secondary maximum is about 1 mm wide.
common_mistakes: Treating \( a\sin\theta=n\lambda \) as the condition for maxima, by analogy with Young's formula
Taking the central maximum as the same width as a secondary maximum
Including \( n=0 \) as a minimum
Forgetting that a narrower slit gives a wider pattern

topics.name: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
topics.summary: Even a perfect lens cannot form a point image of a point source, because diffraction at its circular aperture spreads the light into a small disc. Rayleigh's criterion says two points are just resolved when the central maximum of one image falls on the first minimum of the other. For a telescope of objective diameter \( D \), this gives the limiting angle \( \Delta\theta=1.22\lambda/D \); the factor 1.22 comes from the circular shape of the aperture. Resolving power is the reciprocal of the limit of resolution, so a larger aperture or a shorter wavelength always resolves better. For a microscope, the minimum resolvable distance is \( d_\text{min}=1.22\lambda/(2\,\text{NA}) \), where the numerical aperture \( \text{NA}=\mu\sin\alpha \) and \( \alpha \) is the half-angle of the cone of light accepted by the objective. Oil immersion raises \( \mu \) and so improves resolution. In air NA cannot exceed 1. Magnification by an eyepiece cannot resolve detail that the objective has already blurred.
topics.worked_example: A telescope with \( D=2.44 \) m observes at \( \lambda=500 \) nm: \( \Delta\theta=\dfrac{1.22\times500\times10^{-9}}{2.44}=2.5\times10^{-7} \) rad, so its resolving power is \( 4\times10^{6} \) rad\( ^{-1} \).
common_mistakes: Thinking a larger aperture gives a larger limiting angle
Dropping the 1.22 factor or the factor 2 in the microscope formula
Confusing resolving power with magnifying power
Using the radius instead of the diameter of the objective

topics.name: Polarization of Light: Malus's Law and Polarization by Reflection
topics.summary: Polarization shows that light is a transverse wave; longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarized. Unpolarized light has vibrations in all directions perpendicular to travel. An ideal polarizer passes only the component along its axis, so unpolarized light of intensity \( I_0 \) always emerges with \( I_0/2 \), whatever the orientation. Once the light is polarized, an analyzer at angle \( \theta \) passes \( I=I_0\cos^2\theta \) (Malus's law): the amplitude component is \( \cos\theta \), and intensity goes as its square. Crossed polarizers transmit nothing, but a third polarizer placed between them at an angle lets some light through. When unpolarized light strikes a transparent surface at Brewster's angle, \( \tan\theta_B=\mu \), the reflected ray is completely polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence, while the refracted ray is only partially polarized. At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are exactly perpendicular, so \( \theta_B+\theta_r=90^\circ \). Polaroid sunglasses use this to block glare reflected from roads and water.
topics.worked_example: Unpolarized light of intensity \( I_0 \) passes through a polarizer and then an analyzer at \( 60^\circ \): after the polarizer, \( \dfrac{I_0}{2} \); after the analyzer, \( \dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^260^\circ=\dfrac{I_0}{8} \). For glass with \( \mu=\sqrt3 \), \( \theta_B=60^\circ \) and the refraction angle is \( 30^\circ \).
common_mistakes: Using \( \cos\theta \) instead of \( \cos^2\theta \) in Malus's law
Applying Malus's law directly to unpolarized light instead of first halving
Using \( \sin\theta_B=\mu \) or \( \cos\theta_B=\mu \) instead of \( \tan\theta_B=\mu \)
Claiming the refracted ray at Brewster's angle is completely polarized

questions.topic: Huygens' Principle: Wavefronts, and Reflection and Refraction Using Wavefronts
questions.question: What is a wavefront?
options: The locus of all points that oscillate in the same phase
The straight line along which light energy travels
The locus of points having maximum amplitude only
The boundary surface separating two media
questions.explanation:
A wavefront is a surface on which every point has the same phase of oscillation.

The direction of energy flow (the ray) is perpendicular to this surface.
questions.hint: Think of the word 'phase': what do all points on a wavefront share?
distractor_logic: That describes a ray, which is always perpendicular to the wavefront, not the wavefront itself
Confuses a wavefront with a crest; a wavefront is defined by equal phase, not by maximum displacement

questions.topic: Huygens' Principle: Wavefronts, and Reflection and Refraction Using Wavefronts
questions.question: A point source of light is placed close to an observer. What is the shape of the wavefront near the source?
questions.explanation:
From a point source, light travels equally in all directions in a uniform medium.

So all points at the same distance \( r \) share the same phase, forming a sphere of radius \( r \).
questions.hint: In a uniform medium, light from a point spreads equally in every direction.
distractor_logic: A plane wavefront appears only very far from the source, where a small part of a huge sphere looks flat
A cylindrical wavefront comes from a line source such as a slit, not from a point source
Light spreads equally in all directions from a point source in a uniform medium, so there is no reason for an elliptical shape

questions.topic: Huygens' Principle: Wavefronts, and Reflection and Refraction Using Wavefronts
questions.question: Light from a very distant star reaches the Earth. What type of wavefront arrives at a telescope?
questions.explanation:
A star is a point source, so its wavefront starts spherical.

At a very large distance the radius is huge, and a small portion of a huge sphere is practically flat, so a plane wavefront reaches the telescope.
questions.hint: What does a small patch of a gigantic sphere look like?
distractor_logic: The sphere has an enormous radius by the time it reaches Earth, so over a small aperture it is effectively flat
Cylindrical wavefronts come from line sources such as a long slit, not from a distant star
No standard source produces a conical wavefront in this situation

questions.topic: Huygens' Principle: Wavefronts, and Reflection and Refraction Using Wavefronts
questions.question: What is the angle between a ray of light and the wavefront at the point where they meet?
options: It varies from point to point randomly
questions.explanation:
The ray shows the direction in which the wavefront advances.

A wavefront advances along its normal, so the ray is perpendicular to it, making \( 90^\circ \).
questions.hint: A wavefront moves forward along its own normal.
distractor_logic: A ray lying along the wavefront would mean energy flows sideways along a surface of equal phase, which does not happen
There is no special role for \( 45^\circ \); the ray is the normal to the wavefront
In an isotropic medium the ray is always along the normal to the wavefront, so the angle is fixed

questions.topic: Huygens' Principle: Wavefronts, and Reflection and Refraction Using Wavefronts
questions.question: According to Huygens' principle, how is the new position of a wavefront found after a short time \( t \)?
options: As the common tangent (forward envelope) to all the secondary wavelets
As the sum of all the secondary wavelets added together
As the average position of all the secondary wavelets
As the backward envelope of the secondary wavelets
questions.explanation:
Every point on the wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out with the wave speed \( v \).

After time \( t \) each wavelet has radius \( vt \).

The surface that touches all these wavelets in the forward direction (the common tangent) is the new wavefront.
questions.hint: Imagine drawing small circles from every point and then a single surface just touching them all.
distractor_logic: Adding the wavelets is not Huygens' construction; the new wavefront is the surface that touches all the wavelets
Averaging positions has no physical meaning here; the envelope (common tangent) is used
Huygens assumed the backward wave is absent, so only the forward envelope is taken

questions.question: A long, narrow illuminated slit acts as a line source. What shape of wavefront does it produce?
questions.explanation:
Points at equal perpendicular distance from a line lie on a cylinder around it.

So a line source produces cylindrical wavefronts.
questions.hint: Which surface is at equal distance from a straight line?

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: Two light sources are called coherent when they have:
options: The same frequency and a constant phase difference
The same amplitude, whatever their phase relation
The same intensity but a randomly changing phase difference
questions.explanation:
A steady interference pattern needs the phase difference between the two waves to stay constant.

That requires the same frequency and a fixed phase relation; such sources are coherent.
questions.hint: What must stay fixed for bright and dark fringes to stay in place?
distractor_logic: Equal amplitude alone is not enough; the phase difference must stay fixed in time
A randomly changing phase difference washes out the fringes, which is exactly what incoherence means
Different frequencies make the phase difference change continuously, so no steady pattern forms

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: In Young's double slit experiment, a bright fringe is formed at points where the path difference \( \Delta \) equals:
questions.explanation:
For constructive interference the two waves must meet crest on crest.

That happens when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: \( \Delta=n\lambda \).
questions.hint: Crest meets crest when the extra distance is a whole number of wavelengths.
distractor_logic: This is the condition for a dark fringe; the two conditions have been swapped
A quarter-wavelength path difference gives neither complete reinforcement nor complete cancellation
The bright-fringe condition is linear in \( n \), giving equally spaced fringes

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: In Young's double slit experiment, a dark fringe is formed where the path difference \( \Delta \) equals:
questions.explanation:
For destructive interference a crest must meet a trough.

That needs an odd number of half wavelengths: \( \Delta=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda \).
questions.hint: Crest meets trough when the extra distance is half a wavelength more than a whole number.
distractor_logic: This is the bright-fringe condition; the two conditions have been swapped
This is still a whole number of wavelengths, which gives reinforcement, not cancellation
Even multiples of \( \lambda \) are whole wavelengths, which give bright fringes

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: Which expression gives the fringe width \( \beta \) in Young's double slit experiment? (\( d \) = slit separation, \( D \) = slit-to-screen distance)
questions.explanation:
Bright fringes lie at \( y_n=\dfrac{n\lambda D}{d} \).

The spacing between neighbours is \( \beta=y_{n+1}-y_n=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \).
questions.hint: Fringes spread out more on a farther screen and with longer wavelength.
distractor_logic: Swaps \( d \) and \( D \); a larger slit separation actually gives narrower fringes
Inverts the whole relation; longer wavelength must give wider fringes, not narrower
The units come out wrong; fringe width must be a length

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: In Young's experiment, red light is replaced by blue light, everything else unchanged. What happens to the fringes?
questions.explanation:
\( \beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \), so \( \beta \) is proportional to \( \lambda \).

\( \lambda_\text{blue}<\lambda_\text{red} \), so the fringes become narrower.
questions.hint: Which colour has the shorter wavelength?
distractor_logic: Blue has a shorter wavelength, and \( \beta \) is proportional to \( \lambda \), so the fringes shrink
Fringe width depends directly on wavelength, so changing colour must change it
Blue light from the same arrangement is still coherent, so fringes still form

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: Two separate electric bulbs placed side by side do not produce an interference pattern. Why?
options: Their combined intensity is too high for fringes to form
They are not coherent: the phase difference between their light changes randomly and very rapidly
Light from bulbs does not obey the principle of superposition
Each bulb emits only one wavelength
questions.explanation:
Each bulb emits from countless atoms at random times, so the phase difference changes about every \( 10^{-8} \) s or faster.

The fringes move so quickly that the eye sees only uniform illumination.
questions.hint: What must stay constant between two sources for steady fringes?
distractor_logic: Brightness does not prevent interference; a fixed phase relation is what matters
Superposition always holds for light; the fringes shift too fast to be seen
Bulbs emit many wavelengths, and in any case a single wavelength would help rather than prevent fringes

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: At the centre of the screen in Young's double slit experiment, where the path difference is zero, the fringe is:
options: Bright for some wavelengths and dark for others
Neither bright nor dark, always half intensity
questions.explanation:
At the centre the two paths are equal, so \( \Delta=0=0\cdot\lambda \).

That satisfies the bright-fringe condition with \( n=0 \), for any wavelength.
questions.hint: Put \( \Delta=0 \) into the bright-fringe condition.
distractor_logic: Zero path difference means the waves arrive in step, so they reinforce
\( \Delta=0 \) is \( n=0 \) in \( \Delta=n\lambda \) for every wavelength, so it is always bright
Waves in step give full reinforcement, not half intensity

questions.topic: Interference of Light: Coherent Sources and Young's Double Slit Experiment
questions.question: In Young's experiment the separation \( d \) between the slits is increased. What happens to the fringe width?
options: It doubles, whatever the change in \( d \)
questions.explanation:
\( \beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \), so \( \beta \) is inversely proportional to \( d \).

Increasing \( d \) therefore makes the fringes narrower.
questions.hint: Where does \( d \) appear in the fringe-width formula?
distractor_logic: Reverses the dependence; \( d \) is in the denominator of \( \beta=\lambda D/d \)
Fringe width depends on \( d \), so it must change
The change depends on how much \( d \) changes, and the fringe width in fact goes down

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: What is diffraction of light?
options: The bending of light around the edges of an obstacle or aperture into the region of geometrical shadow
The splitting of white light into its colours
The bending of light at the boundary between two media due to a change of speed
The bouncing back of light from a smooth surface
questions.explanation:
When a wave meets an edge or a small opening, the secondary wavelets from the unobstructed part spread into the shadow region.

This spreading and bending around edges is diffraction.
questions.hint: Think of waves spreading after passing through a narrow gap.
distractor_logic: That is dispersion, caused by \( \mu \) depending on wavelength
That is refraction, which happens at an interface, not at an edge
That is reflection

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: For single slit diffraction with slit width \( a \), the condition \( a\sin\theta=n\lambda \) (\( n=\pm1,\pm2,\ldots \)) gives the positions of:
options: Points of maximum intensity, including \( n=0 \)
questions.explanation:
Divide the slit into two halves. When \( a\sin\theta=\lambda \), each point in the upper half pairs with a point in the lower half with path difference \( \lambda/2 \), so all pairs cancel.

The same pairing works for \( a\sin\theta=n\lambda \), so these angles are dark.
questions.hint: For a single slit, whole wavelengths across the slit lead to cancellation, not reinforcement.
distractor_logic: False analogy with Young's formula \( d\sin\theta=n\lambda \); for a single slit this same-looking condition gives minima
The central maximum is at \( \theta=0 \), which is not given by this condition since \( n\neq0 \) here
\( n=0 \) is excluded, and the condition marks minima, not maxima

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: In a single slit diffraction pattern, how does the width of the central maximum compare with the width of each secondary maximum?
options: It is four times as wide
questions.explanation:
Minima are at \( \theta=\pm\dfrac{\lambda}{a},\pm\dfrac{2\lambda}{a},\ldots \)

The central maximum lies between \( -\dfrac{\lambda}{a} \) and \( +\dfrac{\lambda}{a} \): width \( \dfrac{2\lambda}{a} \).

Each secondary maximum lies between neighbouring minima: width \( \dfrac{\lambda}{a} \).
questions.hint: Count how many minimum-to-minimum gaps the central maximum covers.
distractor_logic: Ignores that the central maximum stretches from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other
The central maximum is the widest, not the narrowest, part of the pattern
Overestimates; the central maximum spans \( 2\lambda/a \) against \( \lambda/a \) for each secondary maximum

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: Diffraction of light through a slit becomes clearly noticeable when the slit width is:
options: Much larger than the wavelength of light
Anything at all; the slit width has no effect
Comparable to the wavelength of light
questions.explanation:
The spreading angle is about \( \dfrac{\lambda}{a} \).

It becomes noticeable only when \( a \) is not much larger than \( \lambda \).
questions.hint: Look at the angle \( \lambda/a \): when is it large?
distractor_logic: A very wide slit lets light pass almost as straight rays, so the spreading \( \lambda/a \) is tiny
A slit of zero width lets no light through at all
The spreading angle \( \lambda/a \) clearly depends on the slit width

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: Which part of a single slit diffraction pattern is the brightest?
questions.explanation:
At \( \theta=0 \) all secondary wavelets from the slit arrive in phase and add fully.

At the secondary maxima only a fraction of the slit is left uncancelled, so they are much dimmer.
questions.hint: Where do all wavelets from the slit arrive in step?
distractor_logic: Secondary maxima are much dimmer because most wavelets partly cancel there
Equal brightness is a feature of ideal double slit fringes, not single slit diffraction
Intensity falls off as we go outward, so the outermost maxima are the faintest

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: What is the angular width of the central maximum in single slit diffraction with slit width \( a \)?
questions.explanation:
The first minima are at \( \theta=\pm\dfrac{\lambda}{a} \).

The central maximum spans between them: \( \dfrac{\lambda}{a}-\left(-\dfrac{\lambda}{a}\right)=\dfrac{2\lambda}{a} \).
questions.hint: Measure from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other.
distractor_logic: That is the width of a secondary maximum, or the angle to the first minimum on one side only
Too small by a factor of 4; the central maximum spans from \( -\lambda/a \) to \( +\lambda/a \)
Inverted ratio; a wider slit must give a narrower pattern

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: The width of a single slit is reduced, keeping the wavelength the same. What happens to the central maximum?
questions.explanation:
Angular width of the central maximum \( =\dfrac{2\lambda}{a} \).

Smaller \( a \) gives a larger angle, so the central maximum spreads out.
questions.hint: \( a \) is in the denominator.
distractor_logic: Reverses the dependence; the width \( 2\lambda/a \) grows as \( a \) shrinks
The width depends on \( a \), so it must change
A narrower slit spreads light more, it does not remove the central maximum

questions.topic: Diffraction of Light: Single Slit Diffraction Pattern
questions.question: We can hear someone talking from behind a door, but we cannot see them. What is the main reason?
options: Light travels much faster than sound
Sound wavelengths are comparable to the size of a doorway, while light wavelengths are far smaller
questions.explanation:
Diffraction is significant when the wavelength is comparable to the opening.

Sound wavelengths are around a metre, like a doorway; visible light wavelengths are about \( 5\times10^{-7} \) m, so light hardly bends round the door.
questions.hint: Compare each wavelength with the width of the doorway.
distractor_logic: Speed does not decide how much a wave bends round an edge; wavelength compared with opening size does
Longitudinal or transverse nature does not decide the amount of diffraction
Light does diffract, but only noticeably through very small openings

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: What is the limit of resolution (minimum resolvable angle) of a telescope with objective diameter \( D \)?
questions.explanation:
Diffraction at the circular objective spreads each star image into a disc whose first dark ring is at \( \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D} \).

By Rayleigh's criterion this is the smallest angle between two resolvable stars.
questions.hint: The limiting angle must shrink as the lens gets bigger.
distractor_logic: That is the resolving power, the reciprocal of the limiting angle
Inverted \( \lambda \) and \( D \); a bigger lens would then resolve worse
The factor 1.22 multiplies \( \lambda \); it is not in the denominator

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: The diameter of a telescope objective is increased. What happens to its resolution?
options: It becomes worse: the limiting angle becomes larger
It improves: the limiting angle becomes smaller
It does not change; only the brightness changes
It improves only if the eyepiece is also changed
questions.explanation:
\( \Delta\theta=\dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D} \), so a larger \( D \) gives a smaller \( \Delta\theta \).

A smaller limiting angle means finer detail can be separated.
questions.hint: Where is \( D \) in the limiting-angle formula?
distractor_logic: Reverses the dependence; \( D \) is in the denominator of \( 1.22\lambda/D \)
A bigger aperture also reduces diffraction spreading, so resolution changes too
Resolution is set by the objective aperture; the eyepiece only magnifies

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: How is the resolving power of an optical instrument defined?
options: As equal to its limit of resolution
As the reciprocal of its limit of resolution
As the ratio of its focal lengths
questions.explanation:
Limit of resolution is the smallest separation (or angle) that can be distinguished.

Resolving power \( =\dfrac{1}{\text{limit of resolution}} \), so a smaller limit means a larger resolving power.
questions.hint: The better an instrument resolves, the smaller its limit and the larger its power.
distractor_logic: Magnification enlarges the image but cannot separate details blurred by diffraction
A smaller limit of resolution means better resolving, so the two cannot be equal; they are reciprocals
The focal-length ratio gives magnifying power of a telescope, not resolving power

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: Why are research telescopes built with very large objectives?
options: Only to reduce the wavelength of incoming light
To make the diffraction pattern of each star wider
To reduce the limiting angle \( \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D} \) and so increase resolving power, besides gathering more light
questions.explanation:
The limiting angle \( \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D} \) falls as \( D \) increases.

A large objective therefore separates close stars better and also collects more light from faint objects.
questions.hint: Two benefits come from a large \( D \): light gathering and one more.
distractor_logic: Magnification is set by focal lengths, not by the diameter of the objective
The lens cannot change the wavelength of starlight
A large objective makes the diffraction disc smaller, not wider

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: Blue light is used instead of red light in a microscope. What happens to its resolving power?
questions.explanation:
Minimum resolvable distance \( d_\text{min}=\dfrac{1.22\lambda}{2\,\text{NA}} \) is proportional to \( \lambda \).

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: What physical effect sets the ultimate limit to the resolving power of a lens?
options: Dispersion of light by the glass
Diffraction of light at the lens aperture
Polarization of light by the lens surface
Total internal reflection inside the lens
questions.explanation:
Even a perfect lens spreads the light from a point into a small disc because of diffraction at its circular edge.

Two points closer than this disc size merge, so diffraction sets the limit.
questions.hint: A perfect lens still cannot make a point image of a point source. Why?
distractor_logic: Dispersion causes coloured fringes, which can be corrected; the diffraction limit cannot be removed
Polarization does not blur point images into discs

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: In an oil-immersion microscope, oil of high refractive index fills the gap between the objective and the specimen. Why does this improve resolution?
options: It increases the wavelength of light, improving resolution
It increases the numerical aperture, which reduces the minimum resolvable distance
It only increases the brightness of the image
questions.explanation:
Numerical aperture \( \text{NA}=\mu\sin\alpha \), where \( \alpha \) is the half-angle of the cone of light accepted by the objective.

Oil raises \( \mu \), so NA rises and \( d_\text{min}=\dfrac{1.22\lambda}{2\,\text{NA}} \) falls.

questions.topic: Resolving Power of Microscopes and Telescopes
questions.question: According to Rayleigh's criterion, two point sources are just resolved when:
options: The central maxima of the two images coincide exactly
The first minima of the two images coincide
The two images do not overlap at all
The central maximum of one image falls on the first minimum of the other
questions.explanation:

questions.topic: Polarization of Light: Malus's Law and Polarization by Reflection
questions.question: The fact that light can be polarized shows that light is:
options: A wave that needs a material medium
questions.explanation:

questions.topic: Polarization of Light: Malus's Law and Polarization by Reflection
questions.question: Unpolarized light of intensity \( I_0 \) passes through a single ideal polarizer. What is the transmitted intensity?
options: \( I_0\cos^2\theta \), depending on the polarizer's orientation
questions.explanation:
Unpolarized light has vibrations equally spread over all directions.

questions.question: Polarized light of intensity \( I_0 \) falls on an analyzer whose axis makes angle \( \theta \) with the polarization direction. What is the transmitted intensity by Malus's law?
questions.explanation:

questions.question: Which relation is Brewster's law for light going from air into a medium of refractive index \( \mu \)?

questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters water of refractive index \( \mu=\dfrac{4}{3} \). What is its wavelength in water?
questions.explanation:
Frequency stays the same, and \( v \) drops by the factor \( \mu \), so \( \lambda \) also drops by \( \mu \).

questions.question: When light passes from one medium into another, which quantity remains unchanged?
options: Direction of travel for every angle of incidence
questions.explanation:
The frequency is set by the source and the boundary cannot change how many waves arrive per second.

Speed and wavelength both change by the factor \( \mu \), while frequency stays the same.

questions.question: Using Huygens' construction, why does a ray bend toward the normal when light enters a denser medium from a rarer one?

questions.question: Applying Huygens' construction to refraction at a plane surface gives which relation between the angle of incidence \( i \) and the angle of refraction \( r \)?
questions.explanation:
In the construction, the incident edge travels \( v_1t=AB\sin i \) and the refracted wavelet has radius \( v_2t=AB\sin r \).

questions.question: In Huygens' construction for reflection from a plane mirror, why does the angle of reflection equal the angle of incidence?

The incident and reflected wavelets travel in the same medium at the same speed, so they cover equal distances in equal times
The frequency doubles on reflection, keeping the angles equal

questions.question: A plane wavefront falls on a thin convex lens. What emerges from the lens?

The central part of the wavefront passes through the thickest glass and is slowed the most.

questions.question: A plane wavefront passes through a thin prism. What happens to it?

It emerges as a converging spherical wavefront
It emerges as a plane wavefront tilted toward the base, because the part crossing the thicker base is delayed more
